newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia to delay space station module launch.
newsitem.headline: Russia to delay space station module launch.

text.p: Russia has postponed the launch of the first module of the planned international Alpha orbiting space station until June next year, casting new doubts over Russia's ability to participate in the plan.
The United States, the European Space Agency, Canada, Italy and Japan are the other partners in the project.

Yuri Koptev, head of the Russian Space Agency, said on Monday the first module was ready and undergoing final tests, but there was no point in launching it due to delays in building the third phase, a service module where cosmonauts will live and work.
"We have a delay of 12-14 months in building (the third module), but it may be cut to seven months if it gets government funding," he told a news conference.
"We are going to sanction the new schedule of launches of Alpha modules with NASA officials this week."
The first module, which will become Alpha's main storage area, had been set for a November launch date, with the service module following it into orbit in April 1998.
But officials said last week that the lift-off could be delayed unless funds were made available soon.
Koptev said the government had allocated 3.7 trillion roubles ($650 million) from budget funds, including 1.7-1.8 trillion roubles (about $300 million) this year.
"But it is not enough," he said, adding that the Russian goverment had promised an additional 1.5 trillion roubles ($260 million) to support Russian participation in Alpha.
The new plan would allow a U.S.-built docking module to be launched in July 1998, followed by the service module with the living quarters in November 1998.
Other sections of the station will then be attached in stages by 2003.
Koptev said Russian space experts supported the Alpha project because it would help develop the Russian space programme. "We do not have alternative," he said.
The Alpha station is intended to replace Russia's ageing Mir orbiting station as man's primary long-term home in space.
Some U.S. officials have already criticised Russian delays and a senior legislator said last week the entire programme had been put in jeopardy.

"The problem is with the service module, which if not finished on time will unravel the whole project," said James Sensenbrenner, chairman of the U.S. House of Representatives' Science Committee and a fierce critic of Russia's contribution.
"From what I have been able to see, there has not been a lot of progress on the service module in the last year."
Sensenbrenner said U.S. taxpayers were paying $18 billion for the project and that the countries sponsoring Alpha would have to decide by the end of March whether to exclude Russia from the project.
